#405. Target shares rise 7% as retailer posts best sales growth in five years, hikes guidance

Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.

The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.

"[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters.

Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter.

Encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds.

The company also said it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90.

"The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time."

Target shares climbed about 7% in afternoon trading Wednesday.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier.

This year, the company said it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year.

On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives.

The company said it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season.

Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength showed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround.

As it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter.

The big-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and said it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.

It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer said on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter.

Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

#404. Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI

Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.

Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange.

Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.

The stock opened at $111.50 (€101.7) — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the company's valuation at $2 trillion. Anthropic stock ended the first day of trading at $97 per share.

The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion.

This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI,  has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.

Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.

Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.

That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.

#401. Hims & Hers launches new peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

Hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it announced the new products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

The new offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October launched an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a company spokesperson said in a statement.

None of the company's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims said they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy."

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

The company will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

Hims said it plans to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The company also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized plan to their needs, if appropriate.

The company said it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

"If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options."

However, Vinjamoori said there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

"We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he said. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a company of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead."

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He said Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight."

But health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," said Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body."

Kritzer said the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, said Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide users, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler said one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

"With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?"

But he said the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

That appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The company says patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

Hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that says the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

In practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "big fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

There is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

Meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data shows only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

Glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione showed that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also said in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

All of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

#400. Black Friday PS5 and PS5 Pro deals: See the best deals at Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Target

If you are trying to get your hands on a PlayStation 5 right now, the real win is not a discount — it is simply finding one in stock at standard retail price. Between a global RAM shortage driven by the AI boom, which pushed Sony to hike console prices twice in under a year, and the massive hype around GTA 6, standalone console markdowns are nowhere to be found.

Today, the PS5 Slim Digital Edition starts at $599.99, and the flagship PS5 Pro retails for $899.99. Depending on the model, that means PlayStation 5 hardware actually costs $150 to $200 more today than it did when the console originally launched in 2020.

For weeks, the hype around GTA 6 completely wiped out store shelves across the country — especially for the PS5 Pro. The good news is that major retailers like Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon are finally restocking standard PS5 models at regular list price.

We recommend paying full sticker price, because third-party marketplace listings are barely worth looking at anyway — the few that are up are mostly refurbished units marked up to nearly double the retail cost, so we left them off our list.

Even at full sticker price, picking up a PS5 or PS5 Pro makes a lot of sense if you are upgrading for GTA 6 or catching up on Sony's massive library of current-gen games.

The standard PlayStation 5 Digital Edition gives you the core current-gen experience in a slim, compact design that fits easily into a media console. You get an 825GB ultra-high-speed SSD that cuts load screens to seconds, 4K TV output, up to 120 fps gameplay on supported titles, and Tempest 3D AudioTech. If you want the best possible visuals in Vice City, stepping up to the PlayStation 5 Pro unlocks PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) for sharper AI-upscaled clarity, upgraded GPU performance, and advanced ray tracing. While Rockstar confirmed GTA 6 targets 30 fps across all consoles at launch, the PS5 Pro is the only system that gets exclusive ray-traced shadows and cleaner image upscaling in the game.

Beyond GTA 6, dozens of major PS5 titles run at higher frame rates and sharper resolutions on the Pro, and its massive 2TB SSD easily swallows GTA 6's 212GB install size with plenty of storage left over for the rest of your library.

If you want to lock down a console while shelves still have stock, here is where the PS5 Digital Edition and PS5 Pro are currently available at standard retail price:

Amazon — Along with the standalone PlayStation 5 Digital Edition and PlayStation 5 Pro 2TB available at regular retail price, Amazon also has the PlayStation 5 Digital Edition (825GB) + DualSense Wireless Controller Bundle discounted by roughly $22 — the only actual bundle discount floating around major stores right now.

Best Buy — Both the PlayStation 5 Digital Edition and the PlayStation 5 Pro 2TB are available to order online right now at list price.

Target — You can grab both the PlayStation 5 Digital Edition and the PlayStation 5 Pro 2TB at standard retail price while current restocks last.

Walmart — The PlayStation 5 Digital Edition is back in stock directly from Walmart at regular retail price.

If you don't want to pay 2026's inflated brand-new sticker prices, look straight at PlayStation Direct's certified refurbished lineup. Sony sells official refurbished PS5 and PS5 Pro consoles for up to $100 less than brand-new units ($499.99 for the Digital Edition, $549.99 for the Disc Edition, and $849 for the PS5 Pro), backed by a full one-year manufacturer's warranty. It is the most reliable way to shave real money off the console without gambling on sketchy third-party resellers.

You might also spot occasional game bundles at big-box stores, though availability is hit-or-miss. Even the overpriced bundles and double-the-price third-party listings floating around online are largely sold out, proving just how intense the demand still is.

After watching store shelves sit completely empty less than a week ago, seeing major retailers finally restock both the PS5 and PS5 Pro is a welcome surprise. If you are trying to jump into GTA 6 without paying double to a reseller, grab an official unit at retail price — or check PlayStation Direct's refurbished store — before this wave clears out too.

#398. Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

Becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise. Midway through my junior year of college, it became clear that, as an international student from Korea, I likely wouldn’t be able to stay long after graduation unless I changed my major from philosophy to a STEM field that made me eligible for a visa extension. The obvious choice was computer science, which was already my minor.

The switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama. I suppose I was afflicted by what Ian McEwan once called “modern forms of snobbery” in describing a character who, after her bookish college education, came to consider “a man with a degree in chemistry incomplete as a human being.” Chemistry, computer science—same diff. It’s safe to say I did not have many friends in the CS department.

But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced. In the post-Facebook-IPO ferment of the 2010s, this country’s computer science departments were newly flush with a certain breed of striver who in another era would’ve gone to Wall Street. My theory is that many in America who acquired a hostility toward technology acquired it by way of a hostility toward these upstarts. That is to say, they aren’t so much anti-technology as anti-technologist.

In any event, I half-assed my way through a good many CS assignments, which meant I was never in danger of going to grad school for AI. But by virtue of a robust public math education in Korea, my entry into the subject was, mercifully, not too bumpy. If anything, theoretical computer science and distributed systems seemed like a continuation of philosophy.

But I could not dispel the sense that programming was a frivolous waste of energy. Every line of code I had to read, every line of code I had to write, was a theft of the time I could’ve spent reading something I cared about. Perhaps it didn’t help that my first two languages were Java (hideous and tedious) and C (admirable but unforgiving). To this day, Java code is like a poisoned madeleine that brings back unwelcome memories.

After college, my visa dictated that I take a job directly tied to my major, and I found a tech company willing to sponsor my green card. The issue was, it could be any number of years until I got the green card—four, it’d turn out—so I figured I might as well find a way to make programming pleasurable.

The first couple of months on the job were joyless. I worked at a health care startup, which I thought gave me a serviceable sense of moral cover against the ongoing techlash and a way to indemnify myself later as a writer. But I liked my coworkers, some of whom also harbored artistic ambitions, and after work we’d regularly adjourn to literary events at the McNally Jackson, a block from our office.

Then, one day, I discovered a language called Haskell. I was tasked with rewriting a code base using a library that borrowed concepts from it. My vague impression of Haskell had been that it was a difficult language involving a branch of mathematics called category theory. There was something seductive about the intimidating aura around it, and when I tried my hand at writing basic programs, the language was indeed challenging, but appealingly so.

I started lurking in Haskell forums where researchers in the field of programming languages—“PL,” as it’s known—flaunted their lavish command of the language. PL researchers might as well be the poets of computer science: a small community of attentive monomaniacs who engaged in a largely unprofitable enterprise—a rarity in computer science—with all the attendant beef and infighting. The unprofitability meant that, unlike AI, the field had an incorruptible dignity to it.

Soon, to my surprise, I found myself programming outside work. After months of tinkering with Haskell, I discovered a book titled Writing a Compiler in Go. Turns out you could even invent a language yourself. I made a few toy languages, useless in practice but invaluable for demystifying how programming languages work.

There was also an oblique way coding could help writing. In Draft No. 4, John McPhee, the journalist’s journalist, says that he still uses an ancient text editor called Kedit, recommended to him in 1984 by a programmer at Princeton. (“I have never used a word processor,” he writes.) When I switched to a text editor myself, I could see why he’d stuck with it. With open source code, I could add silly but useful features, such as highlighting “TK”—a common shorthand in journalism for placeholder text—in a conspicuous color so that it was easy to locate later.

If nothing else, I came to appreciate that programming was a reliable way to enter that elusive mode called flow, a state in which we’re somehow forgetful and alert at once.

In the industry, there’s a general impression that fussing over programming languages is juvenile. If a job candidate expresses enthusiasm for languages, it could very well be a red flag. Being a “polyglot” is no virtue if you can read a menu in five languages but can’t write decent prose in one. And per the popular and influential essay “Choose Boring Technology,” using fancy, novel languages is at odds with serious, robust engineering—akin to how avant-garde poetics are unfit for drafting legal contracts.

Unfortunately for my employers, I had precisely zero fucks to give about serious engineering. I did, however, give a great many fucks about having a pleasurable time at my day job until I received the green card. I took on projects if they’d give me an opportunity to use a new language, which is a dumb reason, and for the same reason even volunteered to change teams, usually a bad career decision. At the obligatory company hackathon weeks, I hacked together domain-specific languages—those specialized for a narrow purpose. I made a meager public contribution by submitting a couple of low-hanging patches to the official TypeScript compiler. I picked up a few gold badges on Stack Overflow. The years went by and, what do you know, I became a pretty decent programmer.

Then everything changed, as it did for everyone else, in November 2022. When ChatGPT arrived, it was a wild card whose impact on the industry was far from obvious. Using neural networks to write code wasn’t new. Early readers of Andrej Karpathy’s blog will remember the 2015 post featuring plausible-looking C code generated by an LSTM—a precursor of the transformer—which nonetheless amounted to little more than a parlor trick.

I remember tasking GPT-4 with rewriting a simple JavaScript program in different languages. It performed like Google Translate, instantly and passably. I likened ChatGPT to the monkey’s paw from the eponymous horror story, the accursed object that grants your wishes but not without casualties. In dutiful pursuit of the given objective—and only that objective—LLMs produced a locally correct solution while mangling essential code around it.

Then, in early 2025, AI command-line tools were released. At first, what I saw wasn’t so much a leap in quality as a greater eagerness to volunteer help. Then they improved—at this point I should quote Hemingway’s line about how one goes bankrupt—gradually, then suddenly. Within a year, they became massively, belittlingly better at my job.

Some engineers still labor a great deal to remain unimpressed, quibbling about how “it’s good at X but not yet at Y.” Please. The flaws are there, sure, and guardrails are essential. But a better heuristic for their usefulness would be: If you had to choose, for the rest of your life, between pair-programming with a competent colleague and these tools, which would you want? Any programmer worth their salt must acknowledge that they won’t be as useful to their colleague as these tools are. Even if the colleague were Linus Torvalds, I would choose the LLMs, since they won’t give me hell for asking dumb questions.

For someone who feels no allegiance to tech, the usefulness of these coding tools triggers contradictory emotions. I find ChatGPT’s indecorous entry into the literary world intolerable, and I remember feeling a creeping nihilism about the writing profession when it was released. I know firsthand what a reliance on AI can do. As I’ve come to rely more on coding tools to hand me solutions, my ability to code has gone through a swift and decisive decline. Depend on it to write sentences and it will, like a neurodegenerative disease, blunt the finer senses that writers must protect the way pianists protect their hands.

Earlier this year, it was reported that more than 90 percent of code at companies like Anthropic and Coinbase is written with AI. As most people are prompting rather than hand-coding, much of modern software engineering has become machine-operated, not unlike Mitch McConnell these days.

While this may not be the end of programming, it’ll be the end of programmers. To keep calling those in this profession “programmers” would be incorrect, since the entity that does the programming is a platoon of agents, with humans at desks prompting something out of them. A more flattering term might be meta-programming, but it’d be more accurate to say that programmers have become operators of sorts.

An operator is someone a degree removed from the thing they manipulate. (Unlike someone chipping at rock with a pickaxe, an operator of mining equipment never touches it.) Perhaps one way to describe how the nature of the profession has changed is that it’s as if cooks had stopped making food themselves and taken to writing recipes instead. If you’ve spent any time around AI Twitter, you might be forgiven for thinking that software engineering is now about looking impressed by markdown files.

This isn’t necessarily something to be defeatist about, and I’m not pessimistic about the quality of engineering. When coding agents were first released, I wasn’t sure whether this was just another natural progression, since the story of programming is a story of ever higher levels of abstraction. From bytes to assembly to higher-level languages like Python, we’ve built tools to domesticate the complexity. And with AI, we’ve finally handed off tasks that are constitutionally unfit for the human brain.

But as programmers cede control over the final unit of manipulation, programming no longer qualifies as a craft. Hence my disagreement with Simon Willison, otherwise a voice of reason among witless clout chasers in AI discourse, who wrote, “Quitting programming as a career right now because of LLMs would be like quitting carpentry as a career thanks to the invention of the table saw.” With all due respect, this is a flawed analogy, as carpenters working with a table saw are still craftspeople.

This means there won’t be great individual programmers in the way that someone like Brian W. Kernighan was: the programmer laureate who cowrote what is possibly the greatest book on programming, The C Programming Language, by which we measure programming languages to this day. (It is the book that popularized the “Hello, World” convention.)

Another loss is that programming no longer induces the flow state—or it induces a shallow sort of flow at best. There’s still a certain “hookedness” to the activity, but whereas tackling a gnarly bug once meant begging every individual neuron in my brain to do its part, the work has become suspiciously effortless. That hookedness may be closer to what the cultural anthropologist Natasha Dow Schüll called, in her 2012 book Addiction by Design, the “machine zone,” the trancelike state of the Las Vegas gambler.

Even though I’ve stopped coding myself, I find I’ve been producing more code than ever before. The features I’d built for my open source editor in the past were unserious enough that I could bang out a quick program on a weekend afternoon or two. But with Claude Code, I’ve become addicted to making what has essentially become a heavyweight word processor, a juiced-up Scrivener. (My changelog tells me I’ve built 239 features and 17 extensions, mapped to 141 keyboard shortcuts.)

One Sunday this summer, I was disconcerted to discover that I’d spent 10 hours in Claude Code. How do I know? I used Claude Code to build a time-tracker for Claude Code usage. I resolved to cut back. I spent eight hours the next day. This compelled me to write a program, using Claude Code, to block myself from Claude Code except for two days a week, which I of course tried to undo with Claude Code, only to be valiantly defended by Claude Code.

With this borrowed competence has come a total loss of interest in learning new languages. A couple of years ago, an iOS meditation timer app I’d used for years started nudging me with ads, and I resolved to one day learn Swift, the language Apple created for iPhone and Mac apps, and build a simple version myself. But I now know that’s never going to happen, because I’ve already built it knowing zilch about Swift syntax, along with 12 more iOS and Mac apps: The machine helped me fork the long-unmaintained SelfControl into a more granular internet blocker; by reverse-engineering a clipboard manager—I was never sure it wasn’t leaking my input—it built a new one with an auditable security profile.

I suspect, going forward, that I’ll still mess around with code, but no longer as a professional. Recently, it became clear that I needed to quit my day job as a programmer to finish a book I’d set out to write. I once told a writer friend that I’d try to be a mole in this industry as long as I was in it. I did get to see some things while I stuck it out and, along the way, coaxed that green card from my employer.

I’m not too sorry to leave this profession at this moment of nuttiness. But I’ll admit that, after all those languages I enlisted to make my detour more tolerable, I came to appreciate the pleasures of polyglot programming. As humans cede control to the machine, it’ll be a joy lost to us all.

This is the final installment in a three-part Machine Readable series on AI-enabling languages. It may also be the final Machine Readable column, period.

#397. No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal

One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.

Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.

The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.

This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.

The text still includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that was pushed by host Turkey.

It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources rather than fossil fuels, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries.

The draft did mention the electrification target alongside efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally as well as other energy efficiency measures. But Jan Kowalzig, a climate finance expert with Oxfam Germany, said negotiators had failed to "meaningfully" link them.

Kowalzig also criticized the text for not referencing a transition away from fossil fuels in a gradual manner — something that had been mentioned in the final decision out of the COP28 in Dubai several years ago.

"This is insufficient for a climate conference that already decided several years ago to phase out fossil fuels and that presents itself as a conference focused on implementation," he said in a statement.

Another hotly contested issue at the talks has been financial support to help developing countries deal with climate change. Divisions largely revolve around who should bear the costs and whether funding should come in the form of grants or loans.

The second draft called for further discussions on a tripling of funding for climate adaptation measures in developing countries. It also noted "with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs," with the adaptation costs in developing countries estimated at $305 billion annually up to 2035.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The wording on finance prompted criticism from Meenakshi Raman, the coordinator of the climate change program at the Third World Network, who had been "hoping to see much more ambition on the side of finance from the developed world."

"Coming here really confirmed the worst fears that developed countries are not only backsliding but putting nothing in terms of real meaning on the table," said Raman.

The European Union has said it won't agree to higher climate financing pledges because it pays its "fair share" while others don't.

The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.

It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems."

Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the text aimed to communicate that "1.5 degrees of warming is not acceptable and will not be allowed to stand."

The draft also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane.

The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up, many of which have yet to be tested and proven on a large scale.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries said the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community."

The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run on for longer than expected. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.

Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.

On Thursday, Panama said it would block any agreement that does not meet its demands for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate methane.

The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said Panama would "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.

Australian Energy Minister Bowen said he expected countries to bring forward their concerns, feedback and questions in the coming hours and overnight.

"We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus, until we have a plan we can put to the parties on behalf of the countries and governments they represent, and they can say, yes, we can do this: we can keep the world to 1.5 degrees of warming."

The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.

The conference is the first to be held under the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.

Countries are at odds about how to acknowledge overshoot of the temperature threshold in the final agreement, with some worrying that fossil fuel producing countries such as Saudi Arabia and Iran are seeking to jettison 1.5C entirely, which could lead to "backsliding" on climate action, according to AFP.

"It's critically important for this COP to recognize, and this is really the first COP that will likely do so, that we are on the way to overshooting 1.5 degrees," said David Waskow, the director of the World Resources Institute's International Climate Initiative.

#394. GTA 6 Online release update: What we know about when it comes out.

Grand Theft Auto VI was released on consoles last week, with millions of players exploring Leonida on Xbox and PS5 consoles. But one major question remains: What's happening with the online mode?

The GTA Online component of Grand Theft Auto V has kept that 13-year-old game relevant across three console generations, with a recent leak suggesting Rockstar makes as much as $500 million annually from microtransactions alone. One would think that means GTA VI will have a similar online offering available at launch, but that isn't the case. Per a Rockstar statement given to IGN, as well as all available marketing language on digital storefronts, GTA VI is a "single-player experience."

There was no online component at launch, nor has Rockstar announced any intention of adding one after launch. Sadly, that is all the concrete information anyone can provide right now.

However, that doesn't mean all hope is lost. It's worth remembering that both GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2 launched as solo experiences and got online modes later, though it was only a matter of months in both cases. Given that Rockstar hasn't even said if there will be a new GTA Online experience for VI, it's probably safe to assume the wait will be longer this time.

The fact that the existing GTA Online is so wildly successful (with no signs of slowing down) means Rockstar isn't necessarily incentivized to make a new one right away. It also means Rockstar has to decide if it wants to keep two different GTA Online experiences running at the same time, should GTA VI ever get one. As IGN noted, Grand Theft Auto publisher Take-Two currently supports two different NBA 2K Online games in the Asian market; the first launched in 2012 and its sequel in 2017, but they're both popular enough to coexist to this day.

Unfortunately, we don't have a definitive answer on when we'll get a new GTA Online mode tied to the new game, but hey, single-player games aren't so bad. I'm sure there will be plenty of hours of entertainment to be had in GTA VI as it is.

#393. A Power Provider for Meta Urged Regulators to Exempt Data Center Plants From Acid Rain Rules

Williams, a provider of gas power to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency leaders in the period leading up to the agency’s recommendation to waive acid rain regulations for data-center power plants, documents obtained by WIRED show.

The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them.

WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from Freedom of Information Act requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism.

“The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.”

In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment.

In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance.

That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply.

Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program.

In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter.

Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.”

The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts.

Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah.

Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.”

The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.”

“EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added.

Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each.

Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.”

The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low.

Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. A 500-megawatt coal plant, meanwhile, can emit thousands of tons per year of each of those pollutants.

Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. The reporting requirement covers sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, as well as carbon dioxide, the main driver of climate change.

The Obama administration later set up a program that would separate CO2 reporting requirements, though the Trump administration has made moves to repeal that program.

Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says.

“If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says.

Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.)

When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. No one envisioned this,” Jenks says. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says.

Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

“Congress should have the ability and the authority to say, we have this situation, it wasn’t anticipated, here is the law,” Jenks says. “If the world were working, that’s what should happen.”

#390. Krispy Kreme is giving away free Thanksgiving doughnuts today — how to claim yours

Does your Monday morning WFH routine need an immediate morale boost before Thanksgiving travel chaos completely derails your week? Krispy Kreme is quietly running a free promotion that's worth the detour.

Through Nov. 23, Krispy Kreme rewards members (it's free to join) can score one free Thanksgiving collection doughnut with any purchase at participating U.S. shops and online. And if you miss today’s deadline, Krispy Kreme is also offering a $1 Original Glazed Dozen when you buy any dozen through Nov. 29 in the app.

To claim the limited-time freebie, you simply need to buy any menu item (even a single drip coffee or glazed doughnut) and either scan your Rewards barcode in the Krispy Kreme app (iOS or Android) at the register, provide your account phone number in-store, or log in and apply the reward at checkout online.

You can choose from four seasonal flavors: Cinnamon Apple Filled, Double Chocolate Crumble, Caramel Pumpkin, or Berry Cobbler.

Is this truly a "free" promotion when you're being asked to make a qualifying purchase? It's definitely a grey area, and frankly, we're not going to get into it. I'm simply pointing you toward bonus doughnuts, and for that, I will not apologize.

#389. Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?

Russian President Putin has suggested evacuating civilians from the embattled Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka. But experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.

Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

#388. Inside Google’s Failure to Make Google Maps Work for Palestinians

On the road that connects the villages to the north of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, there is always a watchtower and a gate, often flanked by Israeli soldiers with machine guns around their necks. None of these things are visible on Google Maps. Where drivers see a checkpoint, a barrier, and soldiers searching cars, the world’s most popular navigation app renders a clear blue line indicating the coast is clear.

This story was produced in partnership with the Palestine Reporting Lab, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism (ARIJ), Lighthouse Reports, and Evident.

Routes and maps are not just a matter of journey times or congestion for the nearly 3.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank. Drivers there are forced to navigate a growing and arbitrary system of more than 900 movement obstacles, like checkpoints, which can be policed with lethal force. For Palestinians, these roads can be a matter of life or death. Google Maps could help them make safer choices. It has failed for years to do so.

Google has the ability to alert checkpoints, a feature that it added to Maps in some locations around the world during the Covid crisis. It is aware of the problems experienced by Palestinian drivers in the West Bank. In fact, a former Google product manager spent six years trying to get Maps to serve Palestinians in the same way it serves the rest of the world.

Interviews with more than a dozen former and current Google employees reveal for the first time the inner tensions at the heart of the Google Maps project. Multiple former employees described how the company abandoned the effort and settled on a map that fails, and even harms, Palestinians. As we revealed last month, Palestinians in the West Bank have bootstrapped makeshift navigation solutions such as the popular Road Conditions Telegram channel to help them go about their lives more safely—achieving what Google will not.

Rubén Lozano joined Google Maps as a product manager in 2019. He devoted his days to keeping track of hyperlocal driving restrictions, making sure that what appeared on the map matched what appeared on the ground. He fielded emails from Barcelona city officials about small shifts in their emission zones and flew to Australia to document one city’s toll prices. Whatever he missed, drivers were sure to alert in feedback forums.

One day in 2019, Lozano was sifting through user complaints when he came across “Mapping Segregation,” a report published by 7amleh, a Palestinian digital rights organization. It alleged a failure of Google Maps unlike any he had ever seen: its exclusion of the web of road restrictions choking Palestinian life in the West Bank. The report notes the way in which Maps privileges illegal Israeli settlements and makes Palestinian communities invisible. The report described that the app’s functions amounted to discrimination and that this was “not a technological issue, but rather a systematic omission.” Lozano saw it as a challenge—one he was uniquely suited to take on.

“How can we help this?” Lozano remembers thinking after reading the report. Google was the best-equipped company in the world at dealing with mapping infrastructure, he thought; surely he could use these resources to make Google Maps relevant and safe for Palestinian drivers. Lozano worked for over six years to create a more equitable map of the West Bank. His effort cratered in close to six weeks.

“Google has more than enough computing capacity and engineering capacity,” one former Google Maps engineer told us. “They have solved much larger problems.”

A driver who maps a route from a point inside Israel to a Palestinian town, such as Rawabi, is alerted to a border crossing. If a driver takes that same route to Ateret, the settlement next door, the map shows one seamless drive, with no mention of a border. Israel and an illegal West Bank settlement are shown as part of one contiguous territory on Google Maps.

Google spokesperson Caroline Bourdeau tells WIRED that the company has experienced “challenges acquiring comprehensive and reliable data in this highly complex area.” Since the launch of Maps in 2005, Google has specialized in innovating methods to secure the best data from the hardest-to-access places. Over the past two decades it has carried out crowdsourcing efforts in almost every country in the world. Jennifer Mazzon, who helped lead the company's first community mapping tool, says the company had “armies of people” manually adding and updating map information for everywhere from Costa Rica to the Democratic Republic of Congo. In addition to relying on user inputs, Google built out its maps using satellite, aerial, and street view imagery, as well as government data, and licensed third-party sources when necessary. This commitment to completeness has not extended to Palestinians.

When Lozano first decided he wanted to map the West Bank, his direct managers agreed to back and fund the project. But his colleagues warned him against any optimism. He discovered he was not the first person at Google to try this. “It's a very difficult problem,” he recalls being told. People at the company remembered the backlash when, six years earlier, the company began referring to “Palestine” rather than the “Palestinian Territories” on a regional site: The Knesset questioned a company executive about this, and Google reportedly promised to keep the Israeli government updated about any related policy decisions in the future.

Lozano remained undeterred. Mapping the world as it is was his job, he thought. He picked up the pieces of previous efforts and set to work.

Lozano learned that since the 1995 Oslo Accords, the West Bank has been divided into three zones. Two of them, known as A and B, should be administered to a greater or lesser extent by the Palestinian Authority and are where most of the Palestinian population lives. But Areas A and B are small islands inside Area C, which constitutes the vast majority of the landmass, mostly comprising farmland and smaller Palestinian communities. Although Area C forms part of what's internationally recognized as the Palestinian West Bank, the land is under complete Israeli control, crowded with outposts and settlements, military firing zones, and segregated corridors from which West Bank Palestinians are banned.

Google has increasingly preferred to rely on outside authorities to provide and maintain various types of data used in Maps, according to a current employee. In search of reliable information on West Bank roads, Lozano discovered that a former colleague had identified what seemed like the best source for data on Palestinian geography: an Egyptian company that he says held detailed information on coordinates of Palestinian- and Israeli-controlled areas in the territory, as well as descriptions and locations of permanent checkpoints, which the Israeli government has never published. Using Google's internal app for map building and testing, a process known as “fish fooding,” Lozano created a prototype. It was getting close, he thought, but was missing crucial input. He wanted to talk to Palestinian drivers, the actual people the map was supposed to help. “We don't want to launch this just based on the team here in Seattle,” he recalls thinking.

Lozano had previously conducted user research around the world for other projects at Google. He thought this process would be no different. As usual, he reached out to Google’s user research (UX) team with his request for interview subjects to discuss how to improve his product, asking them to connect him with Palestinians who had driven in the West Bank. Typically, the UX team would then coordinate with their external contractors to plan the research. He had sometimes experienced delays as the researchers connected him with people. But he had never been denied, until now.

The UX team told him that Google’s research vendors did not have access to users with experience driving in the West Bank and were not going to look for them. “We couldn't get Palestinians as part of the users to take our study because most of the companies that Google was contracting with would not be able to source Palestinians,” Lozano says. Another Google source familiar with UX projects and the region says that these vendors would not interview people in Palestine because of concerns for the safety of their workers. Google tells WIRED that it has solicited input on its West Bank map before, from employees who know the region. But Lozano wanted to talk to Palestinian drivers on the ground. Cut off from Google's sprawling network, Lozano drew on distant personal connections to conduct user research. “We were asking, for the Palestinians, ‘What do you want to know?’”he said, “‘What is the information that you want?’”

The Palestinians he spoke with told him that even if the map could not route around Israeli-controlled areas or checkpoints, they still saw value in having a map that gave them a bit more visibility before getting on the road, mitigating the unpredictability they faced in their journeys.

Just as Lozano was ready to have Palestinian drivers test the product on actual West Bank roads, Covid-19 hit. His scheduled trip there in April 2020 was canceled, and he was pulled away from his West Bank work to prioritize mapping pandemic restrictions around the world. This had an upside for his waylaid project. “The concept of a checkpoint,” Lozano says, was introduced into Google's infrastructure. This included a new checkpoint icon and a navigation algorithm to help drivers route through it.

A road closure update on the map sourced from the “Binyamin Council,” which is responsible for governing nearly 50 Israeli settlements and outposts occupying the West Bank in violation of international law.

As the pandemic subsided, Lozano's attention returned slowly to Palestine, continuing to work on the problem when other duties permitted. By the time he chose to leave Google, in March 2025, he felt that his West Bank map was ready to go live. “As long as we ingest it in the system,” he says he told the team, “it will work.”

Multiple former Google colleagues agreed that the work Lozano did was robust. After a user plugged in directions for a West Bank drive on Google Maps, the display would shade the Israeli- and Palestinian-controlled areas that the person would pass through on their route. A note in the step-by-step directions would notify drivers about which areas the route crossed too. He had developed a way to mark and route through checkpoints, a list of permanent checkpoints with their locations for the West Bank, and a plan to display them on drivers' routes using the system built for Covid checkpoints. He was satisfied with the handover: “I’m leaving happy that the person that is taking over also cares about this,” he says he thought at the time.

A few months after he left, Lozano's confidence was rewarded. Google updated its West Bank map. The administrative zones were highlighted and route alerts activated.

Drivers traveling between Israeli cities, on Israeli roads that cut through the West Bank, would be alerted that the route “may cross country/region borders” and would be told in the directions that they were going through “Area C.” It was clear, in other words, that the drivers were exiting Israeli territory.

A former Google manager, who was familiar with the project but asked for anonymity for fear of reprisal, described the new map as a qualified success: The checkpoints were not shown, but nonetheless it was “the maximum that could be done based on the resources that we knew would be available.” Google retired its checkpoint icon for Covid in March 2025, the same month Lozano left, and did not repurpose the system for West Bank checkpoints, as Lozano had set his colleagues up to be able to do.

The success was short-lived, however. Days after Google updated the West Bank mobile map with Lozano's work, Israeli newspaper Haaretz published an article criticizing a “glitch” impacting Israeli drivers. It reported that Google Maps was now avoiding routes on Israeli-built roads that cross into the West Bank, designed to let Israelis travel through the territory quickly. Google responded to the article saying that it was aware of these problems and was “working to fix them.”

Weeks later, by December 2025, the company had retracted important parts of the West Bank map update. Google confirmed this to WIRED. A current employee close to the company's work in the region said that he was not aware of any communication, even internally, about Google's decision to do this.

Now, drivers routing from Tel Aviv to a major settlement in the West Bank could travel without once being informed that they were leaving Israel and entering the West Bank. Although Google's map includes a static dashed line marking a 1949 “armistice agreement line,” drivers using the mobile app are given no notification that they are crossing it. From a user experience perspective, Google Maps made much of the West Bank seem to Israeli drivers like it was Israel.

What did remain of Lozano's efforts were notifications when users were entering the parts of the West Bank that contain the towns and cities where most Palestinians live. The updates effectively amount to warnings for Israeli drivers before entering Palestinian population centers.

The former Google manager with knowledge of the project was unsurprised that Google backtracked part of Lozano's work: A complaint from Israel is all it would take for Google to alter the West Bank map, he believes. Google did not deny this. The company has become increasingly entangled with Israel in recent years through its acquisition of two Israeli companies, Wiz and Waze, and the signing of a joint $1.2 billion cloud infrastructure contract with Amazon Web Services and the Israeli government, known as Project Nimbus, that rights groups claim has enabled war crimes in Gaza. Today, as Israeli military and settler violence reaches unprecedented levels in the West Bank, the stakes of a wrong turn have never been higher for Palestinians there. Yet, Google's West Bank map continues to cater exclusively to Israelis. “Any claims of Google Maps showing bias in this region are false,” Google’s Bourdeau tells WIRED. “We are constantly working to improve the map for all users.” In response to WIRED’s questions about military and settler actions, the Israeli military says that “the security forces operate” in the West Bank “to provide security to all residents.”

Amazon did not respond to a request for comment.

Not only are there indications that the world's leading tech company has in effect ceded the West Bank to Israel; in at least one instance, Google populated its map with information drawn from an illegal settlement authority. Google tells WIRED that it does not have a policy against using or purchasing data from settlers. As recently as this November, a road closure update appeared on the map that had been sourced from the “Binyamin Council,” which is responsible for governing nearly 50 Israeli settlements and outposts occupying the West Bank in violation of international law.

“Israel's changing the facts on the ground, and the map is then adapting to represent that,” says Zena Agha, a scholar of colonial cartography. “They’ll put that on their maps because that's what the Israelis are saying, and then it de facto creates a reality in itself.”

#386. GTA 6 on PC update: What we know about when it releases

Grand Theft Auto VI is available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles at launch (it will also be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming, with limits).

GTA 6 has no confirmed PC release date. Given Rockstar's history with PC ports, we originally thought gamers were in for a long wait.

An October 2026 report from gaming business media site Gamesbeat reveals a potential PC launch in early 2027, which is sooner than we expected.

Grand Theft Auto VI arrived on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on Nov. 19, 2026, but PC players will have to wait a while longer. Rockstar has confirmed that the game will not be available for PC gamers at launch, and no PC version has been officially announced yet.

Despite that, we recently got some good news: GamesBeat reports that GTA 6 will get a PC release sometime in Q1 of 2027. GamesBeat has a good track record with unannounced news like this. According to their reporting, the GTA 6 PC release window was confirmed by industry sources familiar with Rockstar's plans. They spoke with the outlet under the condition of anonymity.

Rockstar and Take-Two haven't given an official reason for skipping PC at launch, but a few factors are typically cited when publishers stagger releases this way.

Console hardware is standardized, which tends to make optimization more straightforward than building for the huge range of PC configurations. Some industry data has also indicated that consoles generate higher per-unit revenue, giving publishers an incentive to front-load console sales.

A more cynical take is that Take-Two could just be double-dipping, hoping fans who can't wait for the PC launch will buy the console first, then buy the PC version later. A PC Gamer poll found that 39 percent of respondents said they're fine waiting for a port rather than needing it on day one, suggesting a meaningful share of the PC audience isn't treating the delay as a dealbreaker.

However, there could be another, less financially motivated reason for all of this.

Speaking to YouTuber KiwiTalkz, former Rockstar producer John Ricchio explained that building for consoles first and scaling up to PC is technically easier than the reverse, since consoles have fixed, predictable hardware. According to IGN, Ricchio said it's simpler to start with tighter constraints and add polish later than to build a PC-first game and then try to trim it down to fit console limitations.

Without an official release date, gamers have had to speculate on the most likely launch window for a GTA 6 PC version.

If you look at several past Rockstar games, you can see that there's typically a significant amount of time between the console launch and the PC port.

Grand Theft Auto 4 was released in April 2008 and didn't reach PC's until December. Grand Theft Auto V was released in Sept. 2013, and its PC counterpart was released 19 months later in April 2015. Red Dead Redemption 2 arrived on PC roughly a year after its console release.

The one exception was Grand Theft Auto: The Trilogy – The Definitive Edition, which launched simultaneously across platforms in 2021. Based on that track record, a GTA 6 PC port, if it follows the usual pattern, could be a year or more away.

A report from The Verge claimed that Xbox would have exclusive rights to stream GTA 6 via its cloud gaming service at launch, a claim that was recently confirmed. The report noted that PC gamers would be able to play GTA 6 on day one, despite Rockstar's lack of news about a potential release window for a PC port. Unfortunately, Xbox Gaming's Chief Strategy Officer, Matthew Ball, shot down this report. Ball wrote on his personal X account that The Verge's coverage led to some "misreporting."

Again, the game will be available to play on Xbox consoles via Xbox Cloud Gaming, but that service faces strict monthly limits, which will make it difficult to play through the game in a timely fashion.

Fortunately, a GamesBeat report suggests gamers may not have to wait a full year for a PC release, though it remains unconfirmed.

#384. NYT Connections hints today: Clues, answers for November 23, 2026

The NYT Connections puzzle today is not too difficult if you have no sense of direction.

Connections is the one of the most popular New York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words."
